headline: Highest risk is medium: OpenBBTerminal’s MCP/API surfaces can amplify Airflow-produced content into downstream financial workflows, while direct prompt-injection and filesystem leakage are limited by the profiles.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Airflow can emit task/output content and OpenBBTerminal exposes MCP servers and stdin/stdout, so a manual or bridged content channel exists. However, neither profile shows a shared filesystem or direct parser bridge by default, and Airflow has no browser/tooling surface. The interaction is plausible but not strongly documented, so I keep it low.
conditions: IF Airflow task output is copied into OpenBBTerminal stdin or an MCP tool call
IF an operator configures OpenBBTerminal to treat upstream text as instructions
mitigations: Disable copy-paste of raw task logs into OpenBBTerminal
Route Airflow outputs through a structured schema only
Add a prompt-injection filter on any text bridge
Use separate operator accounts for the two systems

B_data_leakage.rationale: Airflow has broad network egress, and OpenBBTerminal touches financial and licensed data while exposing FastAPI/MCP/REST surfaces. Even without a shared filesystem, Airflow-generated content can be forwarded into OpenBBTerminal workflows and then out through networked APIs. The pair can therefore move sensitive financial material across components in default-like setups.
conditions: IF Airflow tasks pass financial or licensed data into OpenBBTerminal inputs
IF OpenBBTerminal forwards that data through its API/MCP integrations
mitigations: Restrict Airflow DAGs from handling sensitive financial payloads
Turn off unused OpenBBTerminal API/MCP endpoints
Redact inputs before handing them from Airflow to OpenBBTerminal
Separate credentials and principals for each agent

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Airflow has broad network egress, while OpenBBTerminal has no network egress but does support MCP and multiple instances. There is no evidence of overlapping filesystem write or git mutation, so direct resource contention is limited. The main conflict is coordination around shared external APIs, which is narrower than the rubric’s medium/high cases.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same external API quota or rate-limited endpoint
IF an orchestrator routes both through the same mutable credential set
mitigations: Assign separate API keys per agent
Stagger scheduled runs to avoid quota collisions
Add rate-limit backoff in Airflow DAGs
Pin OpenBBTerminal to read-only API usage where possible

D_cascading_error.rationale: Airflow is an automation orchestrator, and OpenBBTerminal consumes APIs/MCP/REST inputs for financial modeling. If Airflow-produced outputs are fed into OpenBBTerminal without verification, OpenBBTerminal may render or act on incorrect upstream facts. The pair lacks an explicit verification boundary in the profiles, so cascading error is plausible in default workflows.
conditions: IF Airflow output is used as authoritative input to OpenBBTerminal
IF no validation step checks the upstream data before modeling or reporting
mitigations: Insert a validation step between Airflow and OpenBBTerminal
Require schema checks on all Airflow outputs
Mark upstream fields as untrusted in OpenBBTerminal
Log provenance for every handoff

E_compliance.rationale: OpenBBTerminal explicitly touches financial and licensed data, while Airflow is a general data-engineering orchestrator with broad egress. The profiles do not show residency or retention controls, so compliance mismatch is possible when regulated financial data flows through Airflow into OpenBBTerminal. I do not cite only one agent because the risk depends on the pairwise data path.
conditions: IF regulated financial data is processed through both agents
IF retention or residency requirements differ between the Airflow deployment and OpenBBTerminal deployment
mitigations: Classify data before routing it between agents
Block regulated datasets from the pair until policies are reviewed
Document retention and residency settings for both systems
Use separate environments for regulated and unregulated workloads
